sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Virtualization allows one physical computer to provide isolated computing environments that behave like separate systems.
sections.callout: ISOLATE → TEST → COMPATIBILITY → PROVIDE RESOURCES → CHOOSE VIRTUALIZATION TYPE

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes isolation, testing, legacy applications, remote desktops, containers, or hypervisors, identify what is virtualized and where its management layer runs.
bullets: Verify changes before production → test/development VM
Old software or OS → legacy virtualization

sections.title: Virtual Machines
paragraphs: A virtual machine (VM) is a software-based computer with virtualized CPU, RAM, storage, network adapters, and other hardware. It can run its own guest operating system and applications.
sections.callout: VM = a computer inside a computer.

sections.title: Purpose of Virtual Machines
paragraphs: Virtual machines provide isolation, testing, compatibility, flexible deployment, and the ability to run multiple operating systems on one physical computer.
sections.callout: Ask why the workload needs to be virtualized.

sections.title: Sandbox
paragraphs: A sandbox is an isolated environment used to run software or test actions without exposing the primary system to unnecessary risk. It is useful for suspicious files, unknown software, practice configurations, and potentially harmful changes.
sections.callout: Test questionable software away from production → sandbox VM.

sections.title: Sandbox vs. Production Environment
sections.callout: Isolation limits risk but does not eliminate the need for security controls.

sections.title: Test Development
paragraphs: Test and development VMs let technicians and developers build applications, verify updates, test configurations, reproduce problems, and try operating-system changes before production deployment.
sections.callout: Verify an update before production installation → test/development VM.

sections.title: Why VMs Are Useful for Testing
paragraphs: A VM can often be created, isolated, reconfigured, rebuilt, and replaced quickly. This makes it useful when a change may damage the test environment.
sections.callout: Break the VM, not production.

sections.title: Application Virtualization
paragraphs: Application virtualization separates an application from some or all of the local operating-system environment. It can support centralized delivery, compatibility, isolation, and legacy applications without virtualizing an entire computer for every use case.
sections.callout: Virtualize the application, not necessarily the whole machine.

sections.title: Legacy Software/OS
paragraphs: Virtualization can preserve an environment containing the older operating system, libraries, runtime, or configuration required by critical legacy software.
sections.callout: Old application requires an obsolete OS → legacy software/OS virtualization.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Virtualization
paragraphs: Cross-platform virtualization provides another supported operating-system or platform environment, such as Linux and Windows environments on one physical system.
sections.callout: One computer must support different OS environments → cross-platform virtualization.

sections.title: Legacy vs. Cross-Platform Virtualization

table.caption: Two compatibility goals
rows: Preserve older software or OS support
Provide a different platform or OS

sections.callout: OLD → LEGACY. DIFFERENT → CROSS-PLATFORM.

sections.title: Virtual-Machine Requirements
paragraphs: Virtual machines are virtual, but their security, network, storage, and host-resource requirements are real. Plan the environment before adding guests.

sections.title: Security Requirements
paragraphs: Secure virtual environments like physical ones. Patch guest operating systems, protect the host and management interfaces, control access, isolate sensitive workloads, and protect VM data.
sections.callout: Several VMs share one host → secure both the host and every guest.

sections.title: Isolation and Security
paragraphs: Isolation is a benefit of virtualization, but a virtualized workload is not automatically trusted or secure. Correct configuration and security controls still matter.
sections.callout: Isolation reduces exposure; it does not replace security.

sections.title: Network Requirements
paragraphs: A VM needs a virtual network path when it must reach other VMs, the host, a local network, the internet, or remote services. Virtual adapters connect through virtual networking components.
sections.callout: VM cannot reach network resources → inspect virtual networking configuration.

sections.title: Storage Requirements
paragraphs: VM storage holds virtual disks, guest operating systems, applications, snapshots, VM data, and user files. Multiple virtual machines can consume substantial capacity.
sections.callout: CPU and RAM are available but another VM cannot be created because the disk is full → storage requirement.

sections.title: Resource Planning
paragraphs: A physical host must have adequate CPU, RAM, storage, and network capacity for all guests. Provisioning more VMs does not create unlimited physical resources.
sections.callout: The host must sustain the combined demand of its guests.

sections.title: Desktop Virtualization
paragraphs: Desktop virtualization separates a user's desktop environment from the physical endpoint. The desktop can run on centralized infrastructure and be presented remotely.
sections.callout: The user's desktop does not have to execute on the device in front of them.

sections.title: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI)
paragraphs: VDI hosts virtual desktops centrally and delivers them to users over a network. It can centralize desktop management, applications, security, updates, and data.
sections.callout: Employee connects from a thin client to a centrally hosted desktop → VDI.

sections.title: VDI vs. Local Desktop

table.caption: Where the desktop executes
rows: Desktop is there and presented remotely

sections.callout: REMOTE USER DESKTOP → VDI.

sections.title: Containers
paragraphs: A container packages an application and its needed components into an isolated environment. Containers share more of the underlying operating-system environment and are generally lighter than full VMs.
sections.callout: Container = isolated application environment.

sections.title: Containers vs. Virtual Machines

table.caption: Application and machine virtualization
rows: Full computer environment with guest OS
Application and dependencies with shared OS components

sections.callout: VM = WHOLE COMPUTER. CONTAINER = APPLICATION PACKAGE.

sections.title: When Containers Make Sense
paragraphs: Containers suit applications that need consistent deployment, isolation, portability, and lightweight resource use.
sections.callout: Same isolated application environment across systems → container.

sections.title: Hypervisors
paragraphs: A hypervisor is software or firmware that creates and manages virtual machines. Objective 4.1 requires Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors.
sections.callout: Hypervisor = VM manager.

sections.title: Type 1 Hypervisor
paragraphs: A Type 1, or bare-metal, hypervisor runs directly on physical hardware without a normal general-purpose host operating system beneath it. It is common in servers, data centers, and enterprise virtualization.
sections.callout: Physical server boots directly into the virtualization platform → Type 1.

sections.title: Type 2 Hypervisor
paragraphs: A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application inside a host operating system. It is common in desktop labs, training, testing, and development.
sections.callout: Hardware → host OS → hypervisor application → VM.

sections.title: Type 1 vs. Type 2 Hypervisor
sections.callout: TYPE 1 = HARDWARE FIRST. TYPE 2 = HOST OS FIRST.

sections.title: Host vs. Guest vs. Hypervisor
sections.callout: HOST provides. HYPERVISOR manages. GUEST runs.

table.caption: Purpose, requirements, and technology
rows: Keep old software or OS usable

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Test a patch before production → test/development VM
Old application needs old OS → legacy virtualization
Protect host and guests → security requirement
VM needs LAN or internet → network requirement
Hypervisor inside Windows, macOS, or Linux → Type 2

sections.title: Objective 4.1 Exam Trap
paragraphs: The main traps are deciding what is virtualized and what runs directly above the physical hardware.

entries.title: Sandbox vs. Test Environment
paragraphs: Sandbox emphasizes isolation and safety; test/development emphasizes building or validating changes before production.

entries.title: Application Virtualization vs. VM
paragraphs: Application virtualization focuses on an app; a VM provides a full virtual computer and guest OS.

entries.title: Legacy vs. Cross-Platform
paragraphs: Legacy preserves an old environment; cross-platform supplies a different platform.

entries.title: VDI vs. General VM
paragraphs: A VM has many purposes. VDI specifically delivers virtual desktop environments to users.

entries.title: Container vs. VM
paragraphs: A container isolates an application with shared OS components; a VM contains a full guest environment.

entries.title: Type 1 vs. Type 2
paragraphs: If the hypervisor is directly above hardware, choose Type 1. If a normal host OS is directly above hardware, choose Type 2.

entries.title: Host vs. Guest
paragraphs: The host provides resources; the guest consumes virtualized resources.

sections.title: Virtualization Decision Path
bullets: Identify the goal: isolation, testing, compatibility, centralized desktops, or lightweight application delivery.
Confirm the required security, network, and storage resources.
Decide whether the workload needs a full VM, application virtualization, VDI, or a container.
For a VM, identify whether the hypervisor runs on hardware or inside a host OS.
Distinguish the physical host from its virtual guests.
sections.callout: WHAT is virtualized? WHERE does its manager run?

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Run an old environment → legacy virtualization
Run a different platform → cross-platform virtualization
Protect host and VMs → security requirement
sections.callout: SANDBOX → ISOLATE | TEST → VERIFY | VDI → DESKTOPS | CONTAINER → APPLICATION | TYPE 1 → BARE METAL | TYPE 2 → HOST OS
